whyThisMatters: Real security moments are fast — at your desk or on board. You do not get time to research if a link, a login, or a habit is safe. This game trains your reflex for good habits, and helps you catch things that only sound safe.
rememberThis: Fast instinct is good, but some things only sound safe — like a short password with a symbol, old virus protection, or a public charging cable at an airport. When you are not sure, slow down and check before you trust the label.

discussionPrompts: Ask the group which bubble tricked them. Most people get at least one of the 6 trick bubbles wrong on their first try.

Ask why "SMS Code Received" still counts as good, even though a code from an app is stronger than a text. What does "better than nothing" mean here — especially offshore where a text may be all you have?
Ask why a short password with symbols still looks strong to most people, and why that idea is wrong — long beats clever.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: The most common mistake is tapping anything that sounds like security — like "second check after password" (also called MFA, Multi-Factor Authentication), virus protection, or password — without checking if it is actually strong, current, or real. The 6 trick bubbles are there to catch that habit.

bubbles.note: This is still a real second check after your password (MFA — Multi-Factor Authentication). A text code is weaker than an app code because attackers can sometimes redirect your phone number to their own device and read the code. But it is far better than only a password. "Better than nothing" is a real upgrade, especially where signal is limited.
A long random phrase without symbols can still be stronger than a short "complex" password. Length matters more than adding symbols — a 16-character phrase beats an 8-character puzzle.
Symbols do not save a short password. Length matters more than looking complex. An 8-character password can be guessed quickly, no matter how clever it looks.
A public USB port or cable at an airport or hotel can do more than charge — it can push harmful software or copy data through the same link that charges your phone. Use your own charger.

A senior title plus urgency is the classic trick. "The captain said..." or "The director needs this now..." is not proof a request is real. It is designed to make you skip your normal checks — such as calling back on a number you already trust.

Virus protection (antivirus) that was installed last year and never updated does not help much against new threats. "Installed" is not the same as "up to date" — updates are what catch new harmful software.
